items.stem: What is meant by electronegativity?
options: the energy released when an atom gains an electron
the number of electrons an atom can share
the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom
the power of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond
items.answer: the power of an atom to attract the bonding electrons in a covalent bond
items.markingKey: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group; F is the most electronegative.

items.stem: Explain why the H–Cl bond is polar.
items.answer: Cl is more electronegative than H, so the bonding pair is drawn towards Cl, giving Hδ+ and Clδ−.
items.markingKey: Cl more electronegative [1]; unequal sharing, δ+/δ− [1]

items.stem: Explain why tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, has polar bonds but is a non-polar molecule.
items.answer: Each C–Cl bond is polar, but the molecule is symmetrical (tetrahedral) so the bond dipoles cancel.
items.markingKey: polar bonds [1]; symmetry so dipoles cancel [1]

items.stem: The Pauling electronegativities of phosphorus and chlorine are 2.2 and 3.2. Predict the type of bonding between them and explain your answer.
items.answer: Difference = 1.0: polar covalent
items.markingKey: difference 1.0 [1]; polar covalent (large difference → electron transfer; small → sharing) [1]

items.stem: The Pauling electronegativities of hydrogen and bromine are 2.2 and 3.0. Predict the type of bonding between them and explain your answer, showing any partial charges.
items.answer: Difference = 0.8: polar covalent; H is δ+ and Br is δ−
items.markingKey: difference 0.8 [1]; polar covalent (large difference → electron transfer; small → sharing) [1]; partial charges or ions correct [1]

items.stem: The Pauling electronegativities of hydrogen and iodine are 2.2 and 2.7. Predict the type of bonding between them and explain your answer, showing any partial charges.
items.answer: Difference = 0.5: polar covalent; H is δ+ and I is δ−
items.markingKey: difference 0.5 [1]; polar covalent (large difference → electron transfer; small → sharing) [1]; partial charges or ions correct [1]

items.stem: Aisha investigates the bonding in sodium chloride, hydrogen chloride, ammonium chloride and magnesium in a research laboratory. (a) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for sodium chloride, showing outer electrons only. (b) Explain why HCl is a polar molecule while Cl₂ is not.
items.answer: (a) Na⁺ with no outer electrons (or full 2,8 shell shown) and Cl⁻ with 8 outer electrons (one cross), charges shown. (b) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally.
items.markingKey: (a) Na⁺ with no outer electrons (or full 2,8 shell shown) and Cl⁻ with 8 outer electrons (one cross), charges shown. [2] (b) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally. [2]

items.stem: A materials company in Madrid compares substances with ionic, covalent, dative covalent and metallic bonding. (a) Explain how the ammonium ion is formed from ammonia and a hydrogen ion. (b) Explain why HCl is a polar molecule while Cl₂ is not.
items.answer: (a) Lone pair on N donated to H⁺, forming a dative covalent bond. (b) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally.
items.markingKey: (a) Lone pair on N donated to H⁺, forming a dative covalent bond. [2] (b) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally. [2]

items.stem: Which element is the most electronegative?
items.answer: fluorine
items.markingKey: Electronegativity increases across a period and up a group: F (4.0) is highest.

items.stem: Using Pauling electronegativity values, which bond is the most polar?
items.answer: N–H
items.markingKey: Largest electronegativity difference: N–H (0.8).

items.stem: Explain why aluminium chloride exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules in the vapour at low temperature.
items.answer: Al in AlCl₃ has only six outer electrons; a lone pair from a Cl on another AlCl₃ forms a dative bond to Al, giving each Al an octet.
items.markingKey: Al electron-deficient [1]; Cl lone pair forms dative bond [1]

items.stem: Explain why metals conduct electricity in the solid state.
items.answer: Delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice and carry charge when a potential difference is applied.
items.markingKey: delocalised electrons [1]; mobile, carry charge [1]

items.stem: The Pauling electronegativities of sodium and chlorine are 0.9 and 3.2. Predict the type of bonding between them and explain your answer.
items.answer: Difference = 2.3: ionic
items.markingKey: difference 2.3 [1]; ionic (large difference → electron transfer; small → sharing) [1]

items.stem: Omar investigates the bonding in sodium chloride, hydrogen chloride, ammonium chloride and magnesium in a quality-control laboratory. (a) Describe the bonding in magnesium metal. (b) Explain why HCl is a polar molecule while Cl₂ is not.
items.answer: (a) Lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (two per atom); electrostatic attraction. (b) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally.
items.markingKey: (a) Lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (two per atom); electrostatic attraction. [2] (b) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally. [2]

items.stem: How is a σ (sigma) bond formed?
options: by overlap of two empty orbitals
by sideways overlap of p orbitals
by end-on (direct) overlap of orbitals between the two nuclei
items.answer: by end-on (direct) overlap of orbitals between the two nuclei
items.markingKey: σ: head-on overlap, electron density on the internuclear axis.

items.stem: Explain why there is no free rotation about a C=C double bond.
items.answer: Rotation would require the sideways overlap of the p orbitals in the π bond to be broken.
items.markingKey: π bond from sideways p overlap [1]; rotation breaks overlap [1]

items.stem: Describe the hybridisation of carbon in methane and explain the shape of the molecule.
items.answer: One 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals, which repel to a tetrahedral arrangement (109.5°) and overlap end-on with H 1s orbitals to form σ bonds.
items.markingKey: four sp³ orbitals [1]; tetrahedral 109.5° with σ bonds [1]

items.stem: State the number of σ bonds and π bonds in a molecule of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH.
items.answer: 7 σ bonds and 1 π bonds

items.stem: For a molecule of ethanal, CH₃CHO, state the number of σ and π bonds and the hybridisation of the carbon atom(s). Describe how a π bond is formed.
items.answer: 6 σ, 1 π; sp³ (CH₃) and sp² (CHO); π bond: sideways overlap of p orbitals on adjacent atoms
items.markingKey: σ = 6 [1]; π = 1 [1]; hybridisation sp³ (CH₃) and sp² (CHO) [1]; sideways p overlap [1]

items.stem: A research group in Bogotá is studying the bonding in chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl. (a) Describe, with the help of a diagram, how σ and π bonds are formed. (b) Explain why the molecule is reactive towards electrophiles.
items.answer: (a) σ: end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis. (b) The π electrons are an exposed region of high electron density that attracts electrophiles.
items.markingKey: (a) σ: end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis. [2] (b) The π electrons are an exposed region of high electron density that attracts electrophiles. [2]

items.stem: Explain why ethene is a planar molecule.
items.answer: Each carbon is sp² hybridised with three σ bonds at 120° in a plane; the π bond requires the p orbitals to be parallel, holding all six atoms in one plane.
items.markingKey: sp² trigonal planar [1]; π overlap keeps atoms in plane [1]

items.stem: State the number of σ bonds and π bonds in a molecule of methane, CH₄.
items.answer: 4 σ bonds and 0 π bonds

items.stem: A research group in Mumbai is studying the bonding in ethanal, CH₃CHO. (a) Describe, with the help of a diagram, how σ and π bonds are formed. (b) Explain why π bonds are weaker than σ bonds. (c) Explain why the molecule is reactive towards electrophiles.
items.answer: (a) σ: end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis. (b) Sideways overlap is less effective; electron density further from the nuclei. (c) The π electrons are an exposed region of high electron density that attracts electrophiles.
items.markingKey: (a) σ: end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis. [2] (b) Sideways overlap is less effective; electron density further from the nuclei. [1] (c) The π electrons are an exposed region of high electron density that attracts electrophiles. [2]

items.stem: A research group in Lagos is studying the bonding in buta-1,3-diene, CH₂=CHCH=CH₂. (a) Describe, with the help of a diagram, how σ and π bonds are formed. (b) Explain why π bonds are weaker than σ bonds.
items.answer: (a) σ: end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis. (b) Sideways overlap is less effective; electron density further from the nuclei.
items.markingKey: (a) σ: end-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis; π: sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals above and below the axis. [2] (b) Sideways overlap is less effective; electron density further from the nuclei. [1]

items.stem: What is the shape of an ammonia molecule?
items.answer: trigonal pyramidal
items.markingKey: NH₃: 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair → pyramidal, 107°.

items.stem: Explain why the bond angle in NH₃ (107°) is smaller than in CH₄ (109.5°).
items.answer: NH₃ has a lone pair; lone pair–bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair–bond pair repulsion, so the N–H bonds are pushed closer.
items.markingKey: NH₃ lone pair [1]; lp–bp > bp–bp repulsion [1]

items.stem: Explain why CO₂ is linear even though the oxygen atoms carry lone pairs.
items.answer: The shape depends on the electron pairs around the central C atom, which has two double bonds (two regions of electron density) and no lone pairs, so they are 180° apart.
items.markingKey: two bonding regions around C [1]; no lone pairs on C, 180° [1]

items.stem: What is the bond angle in dichlorine oxide, Cl₂O?
items.markingKey: non-linear (bent): 104.5°.

items.stem: Predict the shape of water, H₂O, and its bond angle. Explain your reasoning in terms of electron pairs around the central O atom.
items.answer: non-linear (bent), 104.5°
items.markingKey: 2 bonding pair(s)/regions and 2 lone pair(s) on O [1]; shape non-linear (bent) [1]; angle 104.5° [1]

items.stem: Predict the shape of the tetrachloroaluminate ion, AlCl₄⁻, and its bond angle. Explain your reasoning in terms of electron pairs around the central Al atom. Draw a diagram showing any lone pairs.
items.answer: tetrahedral, 109.5°
items.markingKey: 4 bonding pair(s)/regions and 0 lone pair(s) on Al [1]; shape tetrahedral [1]; angle 109.5° [1]; electron pairs repel to be as far apart as possible, lone pairs repel more strongly [1]

items.stem: Sipho is asked to predict the shapes of CO₂, NCl₃ and NF₃. (a) State the main principle of VSEPR theory. (b) Draw a diagram of CO₂ and state its shape and bond angle.
items.answer: (a) Electron pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs. (b) linear, 180°
items.markingKey: (a) Electron pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs. [2] (b) linear, 180° [2]

items.stem: In an AS lesson in Bogotá, students use VSEPR theory for the species CCl₄, H₂O and CH₄. (a) Draw a diagram of CCl₄ and state its shape and bond angle. (b) Draw a diagram of H₂O and state its shape and bond angle. (c) Explain why a molecule with polar bonds may be non-polar overall.
items.answer: (a) tetrahedral, 109.5° (b) non-linear (bent), 104.5° (c) If the shape is symmetrical, the bond dipoles cancel.
items.markingKey: (a) tetrahedral, 109.5° [2] (b) non-linear (bent), 104.5° [2] (c) If the shape is symmetrical, the bond dipoles cancel. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What are the bond angles in PCl₅? (b) What is the H–O–H bond angle in water?
items.markingKey: (a) Trigonal bipyramidal: axial–equatorial 90°, equatorial–equatorial 120°. (b) 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs; lone pairs repel more, closing the angle from 109.5°.

items.stem: Explain why the ammonium ion is tetrahedral while ammonia is pyramidal.
items.answer: In NH₄⁺ the lone pair of NH₃ forms a dative bond to H⁺, giving four bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
items.markingKey: lone pair used in bond [1]; four bp, 109.5° [1]

items.stem: Explain why BF₃ is a non-polar molecule.
items.answer: B–F bonds are polar but BF₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel.
items.markingKey: polar bonds [1]; symmetrical, dipoles cancel [1]

items.stem: What is the shape of silicon tetrachloride, SiCl₄?
items.answer: tetrahedral
items.markingKey: 4 bonding region(s) and 0 lone pair(s) on Si: tetrahedral.

items.stem: In an AS lesson in Muscat, students use VSEPR theory for the species AlCl₄⁻, NF₃ and CH₄. (a) State the main principle of VSEPR theory. (b) State the order of strength of repulsions between electron pairs.
items.answer: (a) Electron pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs. (b) lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair
items.markingKey: (a) Electron pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs. [2] (b) lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair [1]

items.stem: Which intermolecular force exists between all molecules?
items.answer: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces
items.markingKey: London (id-id) forces arise from temporary fluctuations in electron density in all molecules.

items.stem: Explain how instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces arise.
items.answer: Electrons move randomly, so at any instant the electron density is uneven, creating a temporary dipole; this induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule and the two attract.
items.markingKey: temporary uneven electron distribution [1]; induces dipole in neighbour, attraction [1]

items.stem: Explain why water has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide.
items.answer: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds (O is very electronegative and small); H₂S has only weaker permanent dipole and London forces.
items.markingKey: water hydrogen bonds [1]; stronger than forces in H₂S [1]

items.stem: Place the following in order of increasing boiling point and explain the order: krypton (Kr), helium (He), neon (Ne).
items.answer: helium < neon < krypton. helium: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; neon: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; krypton: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; identifies type of force in each [1]; links strength to number of electrons / polarity / hydrogen bonding [1]

items.stem: Place the following in order of increasing boiling point and explain the order: ethanal (CH₃CHO), ethanol (C₂H₅OH), methoxymethane (CH₃OCH₃).
items.answer: methoxymethane < ethanal < ethanol. methoxymethane: permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces; ethanal: permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces; ethanol: hydrogen bonding.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; identifies type of force in each [1]; links strength to number of electrons / polarity / hydrogen bonding [1]

items.stem: Place the following in order of increasing boiling point and explain the order: iodine (I₂), fluorine (F₂), chlorine (Cl₂), bromine (Br₂).
items.answer: fluorine < chlorine < bromine < iodine. fluorine: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; chlorine: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; bromine: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; iodine: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; identifies type of force in each [1]; links strength to number of electrons / polarity / hydrogen bonding [1]

items.stem: The boiling points of the Group 16 hydrides are H₂O 100 °C, H₂S −60 °C, H₂Se −41 °C and H₂Te −2 °C. (a) Explain the trend in boiling point from the second to the fourth compound listed. (b) Explain why ice floats on water.
items.answer: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. (b) Hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open tetrahedral lattice; ice is less dense than liquid.
items.markingKey: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. [2] (b) Hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open tetrahedral lattice; ice is less dense than liquid. [2]

items.stem: The boiling points of the Group 16 hydrides are H₂O 100 °C, H₂S −60 °C, H₂Se −41 °C and H₂Te −2 °C. (a) Explain the trend in boiling point from the second to the fourth compound listed. (b) Explain why the first compound has an anomalously high boiling point. (c) State the conditions needed for hydrogen bonding.
items.answer: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. (b) Hydrogen bonding between molecules (H on O/F; lone pairs; δ+ H attracted to lone pair), much stronger than other intermolecular forces. (c) H bonded to N, O or F; lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule.
items.markingKey: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. items.stem: Explain why propanone (Mr 58) has a higher boiling point than butane (Mr 58).
items.answer: Propanone is polar (C=O dipole) so it has permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces as well as London forces; butane has only London forces.
items.markingKey: propanone polar, pd-pd [1]; butane only id-id, similar electrons [1]

items.stem: Explain why ethanol is soluble in water but ethane is not.
items.answer: Ethanol’s OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules; ethane is non-polar and cannot.
items.markingKey: hydrogen bonds with water [1]; ethane non-polar [1]

items.stem: Place the following in order of increasing boiling point and explain the order: methane (CH₄), water (H₂O), hydrogen fluoride (HF).
items.answer: methane < hydrogen fluoride < water. methane: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; hydrogen fluoride: hydrogen bonding; water: hydrogen bonding.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; identifies type of force in each [1]; links strength to number of electrons / polarity / hydrogen bonding [1]

items.answer: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. (b) H bonded to N, O or F; lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. (c) Hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open tetrahedral lattice; ice is less dense than liquid.

items.stem: What is meant by bond energy?
options: the energy released when one mole of a compound forms from its elements
the energy needed to remove an electron from a bond
the energy needed to melt one mole of a covalent solid
the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in gaseous molecules
items.answer: the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in gaseous molecules
items.markingKey: Bond breaking is endothermic; average bond energies are means over many compounds.

items.stem: Explain why the H–I bond is weaker than the H–Cl bond.
items.answer: I is a larger atom, so the bonding pair is further from the nuclei and the H–I bond is longer; the attraction is weaker.
items.markingKey: I larger, bond longer [1]; weaker attraction of nuclei for bonding pair [1]

items.stem: Explain why hydrogen iodide decomposes into its elements on heating with a hot wire but hydrogen chloride does not.
items.answer: The H–I bond is much weaker (299 vs 431 kJ mol⁻¹) so less energy is needed to break it.
items.markingKey: H–I weaker/longer [1]; less energy needed [1]

items.stem: Using the bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) C–Cl 340, calculate the energy needed to break all the covalent bonds in 3.0 mol of gaseous tetrachloromethane, CCl₄.
Using the bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) N–H 390, calculate the energy needed to break all the covalent bonds in 0.5 mol of gaseous ammonia, NH₃.
items.answer: 585 kJ

items.stem: The table shows bond lengths and bond energies for the hydrogen halides: H–F 92 pm 562 kJ mol⁻¹; H–Cl 127 pm 431 kJ mol⁻¹; H–Br 141 pm 366 kJ mol⁻¹; H–I 161 pm 299 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Define bond energy. (b) Describe and explain the relationship between bond length and bond energy shown by the data. (c) Explain why values in data books are average bond energies.
items.answer: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of the bond in gaseous molecules. (b) As bond length increases, bond energy decreases: bonding pair further from nuclei, weaker attraction. (c) Bond energies vary with molecular environment; averaged over many compounds.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of the bond in gaseous molecules. [1] (b) As bond length increases, bond energy decreases: bonding pair further from nuclei, weaker attraction. [2] (c) Bond energies vary with molecular environment; averaged over many compounds. [1]

items.stem: Which hydrogen halide has the weakest H–X bond?
items.answer: HI
items.markingKey: Bond length increases HF < HCl < HBr < HI, so bond energy decreases.

items.stem: Explain why a C=C bond is shorter and stronger than a C–C bond.
items.answer: Two shared pairs (σ + π) give greater electron density between the nuclei, pulling them closer and increasing attraction.
items.markingKey: more shared electrons [1]; nuclei pulled closer/stronger attraction [1]

items.stem: Using the bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) H–Cl 431, calculate the energy needed to break all the covalent bonds in 0.25 mol of gaseous hydrogen chloride, HCl.
items.answer: 108 kJ

items.stem: What is metallic bonding?
options: electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
attraction between neighbouring metal atoms’ nuclei
sharing of electron pairs between metal atoms
attraction between positive and negative ions
items.answer: electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons
items.markingKey: Lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.

items.stem: Explain why electronegativity increases across Period 3.
items.answer: Nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases with similar shielding, so the bonding pair is attracted more strongly.
items.markingKey: nuclear charge/radius [1]; stronger attraction for bonding pair [1]

items.stem: The Pauling electronegativities of oxygen and fluorine are 3.4 and 4.0. Predict the type of bonding between them and explain your answer.
items.answer: Difference = 0.6: polar covalent
items.markingKey: difference 0.6 [1]; polar covalent (large difference → electron transfer; small → sharing) [1]

items.stem: A materials company in Toronto compares substances with ionic, covalent, dative covalent and metallic bonding. (a) Describe the bonding in magnesium metal. (b) Explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium.
items.answer: (a) Lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (two per atom); electrostatic attraction. (b) Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and is smaller; two delocalised electrons per atom; stronger metallic bonding.
items.markingKey: (a) Lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (two per atom); electrostatic attraction. [2] (b) Mg²⁺ has a higher charge and is smaller; two delocalised electrons per atom; stronger metallic bonding. [2]

items.stem: Mei investigates the bonding in sodium chloride, hydrogen chloride, ammonium chloride and magnesium in a school laboratory. (a) Describe the bonding in magnesium metal. (b) Explain how the ammonium ion is formed from ammonia and a hydrogen ion.

items.stem: How is a π (pi) bond formed?
options: by end-on overlap of s orbitals
by sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals
by donation of a lone pair
by overlap of hybrid orbitals along the axis
items.answer: by sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals
items.markingKey: π: electron density above and below the internuclear axis.

items.stem: Explain why the C=C bond is more reactive than the C–C bond even though it is stronger overall.
items.answer: The π electrons lie above and below the plane, exposed to electrophiles, and the π bond is weaker than the σ bond so it breaks more easily.
items.markingKey: π electrons exposed/high electron density [1]; π bond weaker [1]

items.stem: State the number of σ bonds and π bonds in a molecule of propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN.
items.answer: 8 σ bonds and 2 π bonds

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is the H–O–H bond angle in water? (b) In VSEPR theory, which repulsion is the strongest?

items.stem: Nadia writes in a revision note: "The bond angle in ammonia is 120° because there are three bonds." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. N has three bonding pairs and one lone pair (tetrahedral arrangement), so the shape is pyramidal with angle about 107°.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.markingKey: non-linear (bent): 104.5°.

items.stem: In an AS lesson in Nairobi, students use VSEPR theory for the species CH₄, BF₃ and Cl₂O. (a) State the main principle of VSEPR theory. (b) Draw a diagram of BF₃ and state its shape and bond angle. (c) Draw a diagram of Cl₂O and state its shape and bond angle.
items.answer: (a) Electron pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs. (b) trigonal planar, 120° (c) non-linear (bent), 104.5°
items.markingKey: (a) Electron pairs repel and arrange themselves as far apart as possible; lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs. [2] (b) trigonal planar, 120° [2] (c) non-linear (bent), 104.5° [2]

items.stem: In a test answer, Mohammed states: "Non-polar molecules have no intermolecular forces." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. All molecules have instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.answer: The statement is incorrect. All molecules have instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Place the following in order of increasing boiling point and explain the order: helium (He), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr).
items.answer: helium < argon < krypton. helium: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; argon: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces; krypton: instantaneous dipole–induced dipole (London) forces.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; identifies type of force in each [1]; links strength to number of electrons / polarity / hydrogen bonding [1]

items.stem: The boiling points of the Group 17 hydrides are HF 20 °C, HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C and HI −35 °C. (a) Explain the trend in boiling point from the second to the fourth compound listed. (b) Suggest why HF is a weaker acid than HCl, given the strength of the H–F bond.
items.answer: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. (b) The H–F bond is very strong so it dissociates less in water.
items.markingKey: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. [2] (b) The H–F bond is very strong so it dissociates less in water. [2]

items.stem: Explain why bond energy values from data books are described as average values.
items.answer: The energy of a bond depends on its environment (the rest of the molecule), so values are means over many compounds.
items.markingKey: varies with environment [1]; mean of many compounds [1]

items.stem: Using the bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹) C–Cl 340, calculate the energy needed to break all the covalent bonds in 2.0 mol of gaseous tetrachloromethane, CCl₄.

Isla finds the following data in a university teaching laboratory: C–C 154 pm, 350 kJ mol⁻¹; C=C 134 pm, 610 kJ mol⁻¹; C≡C 120 pm, 840 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Define bond energy. (b) Describe and explain the relationship between bond length and bond energy shown by the data.
items.answer: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of the bond in gaseous molecules. (b) More shared pairs → shorter bond and higher bond energy.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy needed to break one mole of the bond in gaseous molecules. [1] (b) More shared pairs → shorter bond and higher bond energy. [2]

items.stem: What is a dative covalent (co-ordinate) bond?
options: a bond formed by transfer of electrons
a covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom
a bond between two metal atoms
items.answer: a covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom
items.markingKey: Example: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; drawn as an arrow from donor to acceptor.

items.stem: Omar writes in a revision note: "Metallic bonding is the attraction between metal atoms sharing electron pairs." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: The Pauling electronegativities of oxygen and hydrogen are 3.4 and 2.2. Predict the type of bonding between them and explain your answer.
items.answer: Difference = 1.2: polar covalent
items.markingKey: difference 1.2 [1]; polar covalent (large difference → electron transfer; small → sharing) [1]

items.stem: A materials company in Auckland compares substances with ionic, covalent, dative covalent and metallic bonding. (a) Describe the bonding in magnesium metal. (b) Explain how the ammonium ion is formed from ammonia and a hydrogen ion.
items.answer: (a) Lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (two per atom); electrostatic attraction. (b) Lone pair on N donated to H⁺, forming a dative covalent bond.
items.markingKey: (a) Lattice of Mg²⁺ ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (two per atom); electrostatic attraction. [2] (b) Lone pair on N donated to H⁺, forming a dative covalent bond. [2]

items.stem: Noah investigates the bonding in sodium chloride, hydrogen chloride, ammonium chloride and magnesium in a school laboratory. (a) Explain why HCl is a polar molecule while Cl₂ is not. (b) Define electronegativity and state the trend across a period.
items.answer: (a) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally. (b) Power of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond; increases across a period.
items.markingKey: (a) Cl more electronegative than H: unequal sharing; in Cl₂ identical atoms share equally. [2] (b) Power of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond; increases across a period. [2]

items.stem: A carbon–carbon double bond consists of
options: one σ bond and one π bond
one σ bond and two π bonds
items.answer: one σ bond and one π bond
items.markingKey: Double bond = σ + π; triple = σ + 2π.

items.stem: A student in Toronto claims that a double bond consists of two σ bonds. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. A double bond is one σ bond and one π bond.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: State the number of σ bonds and π bonds in a molecule of chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.
items.answer: 5 σ bonds and 1 π bonds

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which molecule is trigonal planar? (b) In VSEPR theory, which repulsion is the strongest?
items.answer: (a) BF₃ (b) lone pair–lone pair
items.markingKey: (a) BF₃: three bonding pairs, no lone pairs → 120°. (b) lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp.

items.stem: A student in Istanbul is predicting molecular shapes using VSEPR theory. Explain why CO₂ is linear even though the oxygen atoms carry lone pairs.
items.answer: The shape depends on the electron pairs around the central C atom, which has two double bonds (two regions of electron density) and no lone pairs, so they are 180° apart.
items.markingKey: two bonding regions around C; no lone pairs on C, 180° [2]

items.stem: What is the bond angle in hydrogen cyanide, HCN?
items.markingKey: linear: 180°.

items.stem: In an AS lesson in Cairo, students use VSEPR theory for the species NH₄⁺, BF₄⁻ and BCl₃. (a) Draw a diagram of BF₄⁻ and state its shape and bond angle. (b) Draw a diagram of BCl₃ and state its shape and bond angle.
items.answer: (a) tetrahedral, 109.5° (b) trigonal planar, 120°
items.markingKey: (a) tetrahedral, 109.5° [2] (b) trigonal planar, 120° [2]

items.stem: A student in Nairobi is explaining physical properties using intermolecular forces. Explain why water has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide.
items.answer: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds (O is very electronegative and small); H₂S has only weaker permanent dipole and London forces.
items.markingKey: water hydrogen bonds; stronger than forces in H₂S [2]

items.stem: Grace compares the boiling points of several simple molecular substances. Explain why water has a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide.
items.answer: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds (O is very electronegative and small); H₂S has only weaker permanent dipole and London forces.
items.markingKey: water hydrogen bonds; stronger than forces in H₂S [2]

items.stem: Place the following in order of increasing boiling point and explain the order: hydrogen iodide (HI), hydrogen bromide (HBr), hydrogen chloride (HCl).
items.answer: hydrogen chloride < hydrogen bromide < hydrogen iodide. hydrogen chloride: permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces; hydrogen bromide: permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces; hydrogen iodide: permanent dipole–permanent dipole forces.
items.markingKey: correct order [1]; identifies type of force in each [1]; links strength to number of electrons / polarity / hydrogen bonding [1]

items.stem: The boiling points of the Group 17 hydrides are HF 20 °C, HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C and HI −35 °C. (a) Explain the trend in boiling point from the second to the fourth compound listed. (b) Describe how instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces arise.
items.answer: (a) More electrons down the group, so stronger instantaneous dipole–induced dipole forces. (b) Uneven electron distribution at an instant creates a temporary dipole that induces a dipole in a neighbour.

items.stem: A student in Seoul claims that a C≡C triple bond is three times as strong as a C–C single bond. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. C≡C (840 kJ mol⁻¹) is less than 3 × 350, because π bonds are weaker than σ bonds.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

(a) Predict the relative thermal stability of the hydrogen halides and explain. (b) Describe what is seen when a red-hot wire is plunged into a tube of hydrogen iodide.
items.answer: (a) HF most stable, HI least: H–X bond energy decreases down the group. (b) Purple fumes of iodine: HI decomposes.
